# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to interpret natural-language instructions and move through indoor environments accordingly. While substantial progress has been made on benchmark datasets such as Room-to-Room and Matterport3D, most published VLN systems are evaluated entirely in simulation, and comparatively little work demonstrates the full pipeline running on constrained embedded hardware. This project addresses that gap by designing, implementing, and validating a modular VLN-style navigation stack on a Yahboom ROSMASTER X3 PLUS differential-drive robot equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson controller, an Orbbec Astra Pro Plus RGB-D camera, a 360-degree LiDAR, and a six-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a wrist camera.

The implemented system runs on ROS 2 Humble and is organized around five core subsystems: a bringup layer that initializes motor control and sensor drivers; a SLAM layer combining a log-odds occupancy grid with RTAB-Map's RGB-D 3D reconstruction [@labbe_rtab-map_2019]; two alternative path planners (an A\*-based grid planner that served as the baseline and an RRT\* sampling-based planner [@karaman_sampling-based_2011] that replaced it on professor guidance, retained in the codebase as a fallback); a natural-language task interpreter driven by a finite-state machine; and an arm-mounted camera scan routine coupled to YOLOv8 object detection [@yaseen_what_2024] with LiDAR-fused bearing estimation. A virtual-mover node is also provided to allow the full planner stack to be exercised offline against recorded occupancy maps, which significantly reduces the time cost of evaluation.

The report documents the complete engineering process, including the discovery of several hardware-specific issues that had to be resolved before the system could operate reliably. These included identifying the motor controller's non-default serial port, determining the correct launch file required to bring up the Astra Pro Plus over its non-standard UVC product identifier, locating the `base_node_X3` executable in a separate package (`yahboomcar_base_node`), identifying a mutual-exclusion constraint between the Astra camera node and the arm wrist camera at the `/dev/video0` device, and configuring the arm home pose so that the wrist camera looks forward rather than at the ceiling during visual scans.

End-to-end testing of the unified pipeline demonstrated that all twelve integration points now execute correctly on the physical robot. On the task `"chair"`, the system performed the arm sweep, detected the target with YOLOv8 at confidence 0.82, converted the detection into a world-frame goal via LiDAR-fused bearing estimation, planned a three-waypoint path with RRT\* in 0.009 s, followed the path to within the 0.30 m goal tolerance, and completed the four-step arm interaction sequence, terminating in the DONE state. The interface-drift bug that blocked the previous evaluation was resolved by adding an `inflated_mask()` method to the SLAM module's occupancy-map class and by wrapping the primary planner call in exception handling so that the A\* fallback activates on any planner failure rather than propagating the exception. Beyond restoring end-to-end operation, the planner layer was extended into a three-variant hierarchy — a brute-force RRT\* baseline, an HMA-RRT\* variant using QuadTree-accelerated nearest-neighbour search with side-retreat collision escape, and a further variant adding convex-corridor quadratic-program path smoothing — and evaluated over 600 planning trials spanning twenty synthetic environments executed on the target Jetson hardware. All three variants achieved a 100% success rate. The HMA-RRT\* variant halved the baseline's mean planning time, from 61.8 ms to 31.5 ms, with speed-ups reaching 3.9 and 8.5 times on maze and narrow-corridor environments respectively, and was adopted as the primary planner. The convex-smoothing variant reduced a curvature proxy roughly twenty-five-fold but proved slower than the baseline in most environments, and is retained for future use. A separate hardware campaign resolved a long-standing sensor availability problem, tracing simultaneous LiDAR, depth-camera, and wrist-camera failures to a single common cause of insufficient USB bus current; with a powered hub in place, the Astra depth stream came into operation for the first time in the project's history and permitted concurrent LiDAR and depth-camera operation. The principal remaining gap is that sensor stability under autonomous base motion has not yet been characterized.
